topic.subject: science
topic.title: Electric current and its effects
topic.scope: heating effect, fuse, magnetic effect, electromagnet, electric bell, circuit symbols

nodes.name: Current flows only in closed path
Fuse wire has low melting point
Hammer hits gong due to magnetism

misconceptions.statement: Electric current is consumed or used up by the bulb in a circuit.
misconceptions.why: Students observe the bulb glowing and think it 'eats' the energy like food.
misconceptions.fix: Current is the flow of electrons; the same amount of current that enters the bulb leaves it and returns to the battery.

probe.question: If 1 Ampere of current enters a bulb, how much current leaves it?

misconceptions.root_belief: substances are consumed to produce effects
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: In an open circuit, current travels from the battery to the switch and stops there.
misconceptions.why: Students view electricity as a fluid that moves through pipes until it hits a dead end.
misconceptions.fix: In an open circuit, there is no flow of current anywhere in the circuit because the loop is not continuous.

probe.question: Where is the current located in a circuit when the switch is OFF?
probe.wrong_answer: It is waiting at the switch

misconceptions.root_belief: current is a substance that travels like water

misconceptions.statement: The short, thick line in a cell symbol represents the positive terminal.
misconceptions.why: Students often associate 'thickness' or 'heaviness' with 'positive' or 'more'.
misconceptions.fix: In a circuit symbol, the longer, thinner vertical line represents the positive terminal, and the shorter, thicker line is the negative terminal.

probe.question: Which line in a cell symbol do you connect to the positive wire?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or thicker means more or positive

misconceptions.statement: A battery is just another name for a single electric cell.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, people call a single AA cell a 'battery'.
misconceptions.fix: A battery is a combination of two or more cells connected together, usually in series.

probe.question: What do you call a combination of four cells?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: All wires get equally hot when the same current flows through them.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the material properties and focus only on the source of electricity.
misconceptions.fix: The amount of heat produced depends on the material, length, and thickness of the wire.

probe.question: Will a copper wire and a nichrome wire of same size get equally hot?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: A fuse is a safety device that 'slows down' the current to prevent fire.
misconceptions.why: Students think safety involves moderation rather than breaking the circuit.
misconceptions.fix: A fuse works by melting and breaking the circuit completely when current exceeds a safe limit.

probe.question: What happens to the wire inside a fuse when too much current flows?
probe.wrong_answer: It resists the current to slow it down

misconceptions.root_belief: safety devices work by resisting or slowing

misconceptions.statement: A thicker fuse wire is always safer than a thin one.
misconceptions.fix: A fuse wire must be of a specific thickness to melt at the right current; a wire that is too thick may not melt, causing a fire.

probe.question: Why shouldn't we use a thick copper wire as a fuse?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it will break too easily

misconceptions.root_belief: stronger or thicker is always better

misconceptions.statement: The magnetic effect of current only works if the wire is touching the compass.
misconceptions.why: Students often believe forces require direct physical contact.
misconceptions.fix: Electric current creates a magnetic field around the wire that can deflect a compass needle from a distance.

probe.question: Will a compass move if it is placed 1cm away from a current-carrying wire?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must touch the wire

misconceptions.statement: An electromagnet is just a permanent magnet that uses electricity to start.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the temporary nature of electromagnets with permanent magnets.
misconceptions.fix: An electromagnet only acts as a magnet as long as the electric current is flowing through its coil.

probe.question: What happens to the iron nail's magnetism when you disconnect the battery?

misconceptions.statement: In an electric bell, the hammer hits the gong because the electricity flows into the hammer.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the visible movement and assume electricity acts as a physical push.
misconceptions.fix: The hammer moves because the electromagnet attracts the iron strip attached to it.

probe.question: What pulls the hammer toward the gong in an electric bell?
probe.wrong_answer: The flow of electricity into the hammer

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Increasing the number of turns in a coil makes the electromagnet weaker because the electricity has to travel further.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the idea of 'tiredness' or 'distance' to electricity.
misconceptions.fix: Increasing the number of turns in the coil actually increases the strength of the electromagnet.

probe.question: Will a coil with 100 turns be stronger or weaker than one with 10 turns?

misconceptions.statement: Electricity and magnetism are the same thing because they both involve 'attraction'.
misconceptions.why: Students see both static electricity and magnets picking up things and equate them.
misconceptions.fix: Electricity and magnetism are related but distinct; current produces a magnetic effect, but they are not the same entity.

probe.question: Is the force between two charged balloons the same as the force between two magnets?
